newsitem.title: USA: Quiet 65th birthday for Liz Taylor after surgery.
newsitem.headline: Quiet 65th birthday for Liz Taylor after surgery.

text.p: Actress Elizabeth Taylor celebrated her 65th birthday quietly at home surrounded by her family on Thursday, just a week after undergoing delicate brain surgery.
"I want to thank everyone profoundly for the outpouring of support and love," the two-time Oscar-winning star said through her publicist, Shirene Coburn.
She also appealed to fans not to send her flowers or gifts but to make donations instead to the Elizabeth Taylor AIDS Foundation.

Taylor waved at reporters on Wednesday as she was whisked into her Bel-Air estate in a Mercedes after leaving the hospital. Holding her white lap-dog, Taylor's head was swathed in a dark scarf to cover the scar from the operation in which surgeons drilled into her skull.

Announcing the screen legend had been discharged from the famed Cedars-Sinai Medical Centre, spokesman Ron Wise commented: "She has made an excellent recovery. The operation was a complete success and she should be able to resume her normal activities."
Coburn said the actress was spending her birthday quietly at home with family.

The violet-eyed star, who has been married eight times to seven husbands, widowed once and been through seven divorces, has four children and several grandchildren. Many of them had visited her during the eight days she was in the hospital.
Last Thursday she underwent four hours of surgery to remove an apparently benign tumour the size of a golf ball from the lining of her brain.

Dr. Martin Cooper, head of neurosurgery at Cedars-Sinai, said after the operation he expected full recovery. The tumour was a meningioma, about 2 inches (5 cm) across, and such tumours were always benign, he said.
The tumour, in the lining of her parietal lobe just behind her left ear, was detected this month during a brain scan as part of a routine physical examination.

Thursday's quiet birthday celebration for the London-born actress was in stark contrast to the star-studded gala she attended two days before entering the hospital. All Hollywood turned out for a glittering tribute at the Pantages Theatre to celebrate Taylor's birthday and her cinematic work.
The event, which was shown on ABC television last Tuesday, also raised over $1 million for AIDS research.
Her friend Michael Jackson sang a song with the refrain "Elizabeth, I love you."

Taylor won the best actress Oscar in 1960 for her role as a call-girl in "Butterfield 8" and again in 1966 for her portrayal of an alcoholic wife opposite her own husband at the time, Richard Burton, in "Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf?"
But even her most acclaimed film roles have paled in comparison with a pain-filled reality. Taylor has been in and out of hospitals battling serious illness, injury and alcohol and drug dependency.

She has had two hip surgeries and was treated in 1995 for high blood pressure and an irregular heart beat. In 1990 she nearly died of viral pneumonia and had a relapse two years later that led to another hospital stay.

She also has a history of back ailments, as a result of falling from a horse making the movie "National Velvet," including a herniated disk, curvature of the spine and arthritis in the neck. This partly triggered a dependency on pain killers for which she spent some time in the Betty Ford clinic, where she met her last husband, Larry Fortensky.
